source.title: Harvard Taps 5,000 Studies to Show How AI Helps or Hinders Learning

source_locator: Main article, introduction and age-specific classroom guidance
checks: Lauraine Langreo reports on Harvard’s age-specific framework for deciding when AI can support a developing skill and when it can displace practice.
Educators in the article describe the value of usable guidance alongside uncertainty about bringing the recommendations into classrooms.
The framework draws on more than 5,000 pieces of developmental research. Those works are not 5,000 AI trials, and the article does not measure changes in attention.

source.title: Google’s AI push could put NYC students’ search access at risk, Council leaders warn

source_locator: Main report, council letter and Google response
checks: Adam Daly reports on New York City Council members’ concern about whether schools can give students access to Google Search without also enabling AI features.
The lawmakers and Google offered different accounts of the choices the change would leave to schools and families.
The story reports a policy dispute and the parties’ positions. It does not establish any resulting change in students’ attention or learning.

source.title: How it feels to battle with a flood of AI-generated complaints

source_locator: Reader letters, housing investigator and responses
checks: Readers offer different accounts of what happens when people delegate the writing of complaints to AI.
Making a complaint easier to write can coexist with additional work for the person trying to resolve it.

These are individual letters responding to an earlier report. They provide perspectives on workload and access without measuring prevalence or identifying whether any particular complaint was justified.

source.title: ChatGPT’s Teen Mode could deprive teenagers of a fundamental need

source_locator: Essay, Study Mode and adolescent self-reliance
checks: Robin Kirman asks whether an always-available AI tutor leaves teenagers enough opportunities to develop confidence in their own judgments.
Wider access to intellectually demanding support and time to work through a problem alone can both matter for a teenager.
This opinion essay presents a developmental and clinical interpretation. It does not compare teenagers using the product with other teenagers or measure a loss of autonomy.

source.title: Do People Trust AI Assistants Even When They Are Consistently Wrong?

source_locator: Experiment 3, conversational conditions and Table 3; General Discussion
checks: People used an AI adviser’s track record when they could check its answers.

In the conversation conditions of Experiment 3, earlier accuracy made a difference when feedback was available. Without feedback, even a previously inaccurate assistant persuaded people on 48% of the final trials.
These were short factual tasks. The final challenge targeted an answer the participant had initially gotten right. The results do not measure lasting trust or behavior in other domains.

source.title: Right Advice, Wrong Reasons: How Decision and Reasoning Alignment Shape Reliance on AI Advisors

source_locator: Section 3.1.1, adviser choices in new tasks, and Table 1
checks: People wanted more control when an AI adviser could act on their behalf.
Participants selected no AI for 12% of choices involving consultation and 38% of choices involving an adviser authorized to act for them.
Decisions in the follow-up task were stated preferences about hypothetical scenarios. The study did not observe people delegating consequential real-world tasks.

source.title: People prefer AI to human advice in multi-turn conversations but neither changes incentivised behaviour

source_locator: Sections 2.1–2.2 and 3, incentivized decision and advice ratings
checks: How participants rated the advice differed from what they chose to donate.
Participants rated AI advice as more trustworthy than human advice. The authors found no statistically significant difference in pledged donations among the AI, human, and no-advice conditions.
The outcome was a single lottery-linked charitable decision. An imprecise or nonsignificant difference does not establish that advice has no effect in other settings.

source.title: The Evidence Base on AI in K-12: A November 2026 Review

source_locator: Executive summary; student learning and engagement; scope of the evidence base
checks: How students used AI mattered to what they later learned.

In some studies, students who used AI to complete work learned less. Studies of guided practice and tutoring showed more favorable but mixed results. Students’ ratings of AI often outpaced measured learning gains.
The studies evaluated varied designs, subjects and populations. Only five newly included student-facing studies were conducted in US K–12 settings, limiting transfer to those classrooms.

source.title: Teacher-regulated generative AI in structured group tasks: independent performance and metacognitive judgements in higher education

checks: Students allowed to use AI during group discussion did slightly better on an immediate unaided test.

Average scores were 8.84 and 8.64, respectively. The model-adjusted difference was 0.506 points. The study did not detect differences in confidence or in how accurately students judged their own performance.
The short test left limited room at the top, and the study lacked a pretest or delayed assessment. It did not measure sustained attention.

source.title: From cognitive relief to motivational enhancement: associations between perceived Agentic AI Capability and student engagement in systems development courses

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

source_locator: Methods, results and limitations; original publisher article
checks: The cross-sectional study analyzed self-reports by undergraduates in systems development courses.
Perceived AI capability was associated with reported cognitive load, self-efficacy and engagement.
These associations do not establish a measured change in skill or a causal effect of AI.

source.title: Human tutoring, generative AI tutoring and independent internet search: A randomised between‐subjects experiment on students' responses to academic challenge

reviewed_additions.source_locator: Wiley, Method (design, support conditions and data analysis), Findings Table 2, and Discussion (limitations).
checks: The publisher and Crossref give November 13 as the version-of-record publication day.
Table 2 reports higher effort and difficulty under Khanmigo Lite versus the human tutor during the second set.
The support conditions did not differ detectably in subsequent challenge selection. Counting attempts did not measure answer accuracy.
